categoricalControls.reportedOutcome: eliminated A. niger inhibition by S. marcescens in K/K6K/K6M under the stated tests, regardless of same-site or separate-site inoculation
eliminated inhibition in the stated soils/tests

confoundersAndContext: At higher glucose and NH4NO3 amendments, S. marcescens died out in K and K6K but not K6M; source attributes this apparently to pH reduction associated with increased metabolism.
With CaCO3 buffering, glucose still eliminated or reduced inhibition while NH4NO3 did not, supporting carbon competition rather than a generic nutrient-addition effect.
At CaCO3-adjusted pH above 6, NH4NO3 could inhibit A. niger even without bacteria through ammonia volatilization.
Degree of inhibition correlated directly with bacterial glucose-utilization rate across the tested bacteria.
sourceContexts.sourceConclusion: A. niger antagonism by some bacteria in this soil system was primarily attributable to competition for carbon, modulated by environmental factors including pH and clay mineralogy.

categoricalControls.reportedOutcome: S. marcescens inhibition of A. niger spread was maintained

A. niger was inhibited more when inoculated as spores than as mycelial fragments

categoricalControls.reportedOutcome: inhibition increased; 1% glucose reduced the inhibition

environmentalDependence: Antagonism usually increased as pH increased.

implementationDecision.supportedMechanismClass: shared-carbon competition with explicit environment/context dependence
implementationDecision.prohibitedShortcut: generic pairwise attack or killing coefficient
rationale: The source supports a carbon-competition interpretation and qualitative/categorical intervention controls.

It does not provide a directly reusable Petra glucose uptake law, uptake coefficients, yield, shared physical resource field calibration, or compatible strain-resolved growth parameter pack in this record.
pH, clay mineralogy, bacterial survival and inoculation geometry materially alter the observed outcome.

validationTargets: Under source-compatible soil conditions, adding 0.25%, 0.5% or 1.0% glucose should remove the competition-associated fungal inhibition phenotype in the tested setup.
A C/N shift to 10/1 with NH4NO3 removed inhibition in the reported unbuffered conditions, whereas a shift to 15/1 did not; this is a contextual validation target, not a portable nitrogen rule.
Clay identity must change the phenotype in the direction reported by the 1979 study; a model insensitive to kaolinite versus montmorillonite would not reproduce the source system.
Same-site versus separate-site placement and fungal inoculum form/timing are distinct validation strata.
